senses: Divinity or godhood, divine essence or nature.
An admired or influential person or entity.
ety: Inherited from Middle English godhede, equivalent to god + -head (“-hood”). First attested in the Ancrene Wisse (ca. 1225); compare godhood and Dutch godheid as well as German Gottheit.
examples: For the inuisible things of him from the Creation of the world, are clearely seene, being vnderstood by the things that are made, euen his eternall Power and Godhead, so that they are without excuse:
He pauses, as if hesitant to mention the godhead of computer design aloud, and adds, "Maybe even something Apple would be interested in."

senses: A place where people tan hides to make leather.
The business of a tanner.
ety: From tan + -ery; compare Old French tannerie.
examples: The River Avon divides the village in two, and at its centre is a tannery, built in 1918 and still in use, with its frontage on the river bank.

senses: A dry measure, containing four pecks, eight gallons, or thirty-two quarts; equivalent in volume to approximately 0.0364 cubic meters (imperial bushel) or 0.0352 cubic meters (U.S. bushel).
A vessel of the capacity of a bushel, used in measuring; a bushel measure.
A quantity that fills a bushel measure.
A large indefinite quantity.
The iron lining in the nave of a wheel.
ety: From Middle English busshel, from Old French boissel, from boisse, a grain measure based on Gaulish *bostyā (“handful”), from Proto-Celtic *bostā (“palm, fist”) (compare Breton boz (“hollow of the hand”), Old Irish bas), from Proto-Indo-European *gwost-, *gwosdʰ- (“branch”).
examples: The quarter, bushel, and peck are nearly universal measures of corn.
Forecasts are showing no sign of an end to the drought, with corn prices hitting a record high of $8.16 (£5.19) a bushel on Thursday, while soya beans hit a high of $17.17.

senses: A flat fold; a doubling, as of cloth; a pleat.
A braid, as of hair or straw; a plat.
ety: From Middle English pleit, from Anglo-Norman pleit (compare Old French ploit), from Latin plectō, which is akin to Old Norse flétta (Danish flette), Russian плести́ (plestí) and also to Old English fleohtan, which it displaced. Doublet of plight (“plait, fold”) and pleat.
examples: Only the hair as it arched so beautifully from her temples was mixed with silver, and the two simple plaits that lay on her shoulders were filigree of silver and brown.

senses: Any kind of willow.
Long, pliable twigs of this plant, or of other similar plants.
ety: Borrowed from French osier (“basket willow, withy”)
examples: Wattling consists of a row of upright stakes the spaces between which are more or less filled by interweaving small branches, hazel rods, osiers, reeds, thin strips of wood, or other pliant material.

senses: Situated beneath the moon; specifically, between the moon and the earth.
In or of this world (as opposed to heaven, etc.); earthly, terrestrial.
Inferior, subordinate.
ety: The noun is derived from the adjective.
examples: All Sublunary Things are contemptible, and of no Value.
Mr John Puffingham was a patron—a patron to the diversified layers and strata of men and things pertaining to sublunary matters.
Staying at the Kennels was the most significant occasion my little world could offer me, and in order that he might share my sublunary advancement I took Cockbird with me.

senses: Making a transit or passage.
Affected by transference of signification.
ety: From Latin trānsitīvus, from trānsitus, from trāns (“across”) + itus, from eō (“to go”).
examples: For all symbols are fluxional; all language is vehicular and transitive, and is good, as ferries and horses are, for conveyance, not as farms and houses are, for homestead.
By far the greater part of the transitive or derivative applications of words depend on casual and unaccountable caprices of the feelings or the fancy.

senses: Any of several herbicides based on it, such as Roundup.
ety: Blend of glycine + phosphonate.
examples: In previous years Penryn Town Council has used Falmouth Town Council to fulfil the parks contract and glyphosate had been used, councillor Debra Clegg confirmed.

senses: A drooping, tapering shape of ice.
ety: From Middle English isykle, isikel, from Old English *īsġicel, from Proto-West Germanic *īsajikil, *īsajekul, equivalent to ice + ickle. It was assimilated to nouns in -icle, from Latin -iculus—the expected spelling would have -ickle. Cognate with Saterland Frisian Iesjuukel (“icicle”), German Low German Iesjökel, dialectal Danish jisegel (“icicle”), Norwegian isjukel (“icicle”) and Elfdalian aisikkel.
examples: Several days of sub-zero temperatures caused icicles up to 1.5 metres long to form in tunnels across Greater Manchester, Lancashire and Cumbria.

senses: A trained support person who provides emotional, physical and practical assistance to a pregnant woman or couple before, during or after childbirth.
A trained person who provides similar support to someone who is diagnosed with an incurable condition and is receiving end-of-life care.
ety: Borrowed from Greek δούλα (doúla, “servant-woman”), from Ancient Greek δούλη (doúlē, “female slave”). Popularized by the American anthropologist Dana Raphael in the book The Tender Gift: Breastfeeding (1973), where the word is credited to Eleni Rassias.
examples: Rebekah Rosler, a therapist and doula, decided to leave, even though her family history in New York goes back to the 1870s, she said.

senses: A relation between states in which a subservient nation has its own government, but is unable to take international action independent of the superior state.
A similar relationship between other entities.
The status or power of a suzerain.
ety: From Middle English suserente, from Old French suserenete, equivalent to suzerain + -ty.
examples: She was tired of living under suzerainty to her parents.

senses: Characterised by thumping sounds from the drums.
ety: From thump + -y.
examples: Like all talented screamers, Ms. Paternoster also knows when to exhibit a bit of restraint, and the bulk of her vocals are steady, tough and clear, a nice accompaniment to the group’s thumpy, lo-fi punk-rock.

senses: Of a grayish-pink colour, like that of the damask rose.
ety: From Middle English damaske, from Medieval Latin damascus, named after the city Damascus, where the fabric was originally made.
examples: But let concealment, like a worm i' the bud, / Feed on her damask cheek

They had a lurking suspicion even, that he died of secret love; though I must say there was a picture of him in the house with a damask nose, which concealment did not appear to have ever preyed upon.

Hortense, with her rich chestnut locks so luxuriantly knotted, plaited, twisted, as if she did not know how to dispose of all their abundance, with her vermillion lips, damask cheek, and roguish laughing eye.

senses: To destroy (someone or something) completely, leaving no trace; to annihilate, to wipe out.
To hide (something) by covering it; to conceal, to obscure.
To make (a drawing, text which is printed or written, etc.) indecipherable, either by erasing or obscuring it; to blot out, to efface, to delete.
To cancel (a postage stamp) with a postmark so it cannot be reused.
To be destroyed completely, leaving no trace.
ety: From earlier obliterat, learned borrowing from Latin obliterātus, oblitterātus (“having been blotted out, effaced, erased; having been forgotten”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix, of participial origin)). Obliterātus and oblitterātus are respectively the perfect passive participles of obliterō and oblitterō (“to blot out, efface, erase, obliterate; to cause to be forgotten”), probably either: * from ob- (prefix meaning ‘against; towards’) + littera (“letter of the alphabet; (metonymically) handwriting”) (further etymology unknown); or * from oblītus (“disregarded, neglected; forgotten”), influe
examples: That is what distance does for us; the harsh and bitter feelings of this or that experience are slowly obliterated, and memory begins to look kindly on the past.
The seal of Pepi is in the House of Rurutȧ. The god who obliterateth sin, Ȧṭer-ȧsfet, obliterateth the transgressions which belong to Pepi in the presence of Khenti-merti in Sekhem.
Soham's station had been completely obliterated (the replacement was to close in 1965 and is only now being reopened).

senses: One who foretells the future.
One who divines or conjectures.
One who searches for underground objects or water using a divining rod.
ety: From Middle English divinour, from Latin dīvīnātor (“diviner; fortune-teller; soothsayer”), from dīvīnāre (“to foresee, to foretell”). Doublet of divinator. Equivalent to divine + -er.
examples: Saw my future with a death diviner / My reflection in her eyes drew up / My twisted past / Oh, I came unmasked

senses: Slender and long of limb; lanky.
Prone to roaming around.
Having or permitting range or scope; roomy; commodious.
Requiring a large vocal range; having a great difference from the highest to the lowest notes.
ety: From range + -y.
examples: For an accountant, Robert had a rangy appearance.
Her African violets weren't getting enough sun and became rangy.
Janet Gwilherm, who was presently dwarfing the duty desk — she was tall and rangy, like a basketball player — whacked the intercom button and announced herself.

senses: An obnoxiously clever or quick-witted person.
ety: From smart + -y.
examples: Don't be stupid, be a smarty come and join the Nazi Party!

senses: To beat or slap with the hand.
To beat, pound or hammer.
To drive by blows; to drive (hard), to cause to move rapidly.
To move briskly along; to run.
To rain heavily; (of rain) to fall.
ety: From Middle English skelpen, probably of imitative origin. The noun is from Middle English skelp, from the verb.
examples: But Mistress Munro would up and be at the door and in she'd yank Andy by the lug, and some said she'd take down his breeks and skelp him, but maybe that was a lie.
A byke was regarded as a glorious capture, not only for the sake of the honey, but because of the fun the boys had in skelpin' out the bees.

senses: A homeless boy; a male street urchin; also (more generally), a cheeky, street-smart boy.
ety: Borrowed from French gamin (“a street urchin; a young boy”), apparently an “eastern dialect” word of unknown origin.
examples: Here, in front, the deserted street was white and black and silent, under the electric lamps. All the lonelier for two wretched gamins, counting their dirty sous, and draggled newspapers.

senses: Suffering from gout.
ety: From Middle English gowty; equivalent to gout + -y.
examples: When days and years proclaim you’re old — A dottle, cripple, gouty fellow, Then for support you can lay hold O’ the upright of your umberella.

senses: A nunnery, a convent.
A formal group or assembly of witches.
In fantasy fiction, a family, group or assembly of vampires.
A clique that shares common interests or activities.
ety: From Middle English covent, from Anglo-Norman covent, cuvent, from Old French covent, from Latin conventum, from conveniō, from cum (“with”) and venio (“to come”). Doublet of convent.
examples: A coven of witches is traditionally composed of thirteen members of either sex, with one of them acting as officer or priest.

senses: Serving a particular purpose; useful; adapted to a given purpose, especially through natural evolution.
Done or performed with a conscious purpose or intent.
Possessed of a firm purpose.
ety: From purpose + -ive. Compare purpositive.
examples: Irresistably it came to me again that beauty, far from being wasted, was purposive, that this purpose was of a redeeming kind, and that some one who was pleased co-operated with it for my personal benefit.
Most human activity is purposive.
I had a purposive air about me that night.

senses: A poet or bard who is divinely inspired.
ety: From Latin vātēs, from Proto-Indo-European *weh₂t- (“excited, possessed”); cognate with Proto-Celtic *wātis (“seer”) (Gaulish ουατεις, Old Irish fáith, Welsh gwawd) and Proto-Germanic *wōdaz (“mad”) (Old English wōd (“mad, frenzied”), Gothic 𐍅𐍉𐌳𐍃 (wōds, “possessed, mad”), Old High German wuot (“mad, madness”). More at wood (“crazy, mad, insane”) and wode.
examples: The volume is haunted by the death of the vates (poet-prophet) Orpheus, who failed to revive Eurydice from death and was then torn apart by maenads.

senses: Not on Earth.
ety: From off- + world, by analogy with offshore.
examples: She invested in an offworld mining company.

senses: Cooked in a hot, fiery style with garlic, tomatoes, and chili.
ety: From Italian, feminine of arrabbiato (“angry”) referring to its spiciness; see rabbia (“anger”) for more.
examples: Chicken arrabbiata was served on steaming fettuccine.

senses: The lower part of a bikini without the upper part (i.e., topless).
A one-piece swimsuit, which may cover both the chest and the crotch (as contrasted with a bikini, which consists of two pieces).
ety: Borrowed from French monokini or simply mono- + -kini, punningly reinterpreting the first syllable of "bikini" as the prefix bi-.
examples: French academics and historians have spent the early summer months pondering the sociological meaning of the demise of France's once-favourite piece of beachwear, the "monokini" – the bottom half of a bikini with no top.
In fact, the San Francisco Chronicle featured a photo of a woman in a monokini — her exposed breasts clearly visible — on its front page.

senses: Appropriate to, or in the way of, a soldier.
ety: From soldier + -ly. Compare soldierlike.
examples: His soldierly demeanour stood him good stead in civilian life when vicissitudes would assail him.

senses: Together with lauds, the earliest of the canonical hours; traditionally prayed at sunrise or earlier.
Morning prayers.
ety: From Middle English matyns, matynes, from Old French matines.
examples: This chant was sung in many cathedrals both at First Vespers and at Matins for Christmas Day. In Notre Dame and many other churches, however, it was only performed at First Vespers.
The monk must arise when the matins ring, / The abbot may sleep to their chime; / But the yeoman must start when the bugles sing / ’Tis time, my hearts, ’tis time.

senses: The transformation of a society from close identification with religious values and institutions toward non-religious (or "irreligious") values and secular institutions.
The deconsecration of a church.
The act of becoming secular.
ety: From secularize + -ation.
examples: Wojtyla and Mazowiecki come from the same Krakow intellectual circles that advocated the secularization of politics and led the recent efforts for Polish-Jewish dialogue.

senses: Not frightened or hesitant; undaunted; not put off; unimpressed.
ety: From un- + fazed.
examples: After stumbling and landing on her face, the toddler picked herself up and continued unfazed.
The Johnnie O'Briens and the Barney O'Rourkes were there, too, apparently unfazed by the magnificence of the surroundings.
When outsiders heard the melodies of Johann Sebastian Bach in a single-voice, monophonic square wave, no harmony, they were universally unfazed. Big deal!

senses: A small amount of no worth.
ety: Short for diddly-squat.
examples: They head down the mountain, back to base camp, and when they get there they don't say diddly. They don't talk. Not a word, like they're deaf and dumb.

senses: Full of knots; knotty.
Tied in knots.
Tangled, tangly, knotty, entangled, matted, snarled, unkempt, or uncombed.
Having the shape or form of a knot.
ety: From Middle English knotted, iknotted, from the past participle of the verb knotten.
examples: These men lashed themselves and each other unmercifully with knotted leather scourges until the blood ran, two or three times daily.
Grey hairs straggled out from under her head-gear, which surrounded a dark face with bushy eyebrows and a long knotted nose.

senses: To perform the functions of some office.
ety: Borrowed from Latin officiātus, perfect participle of Late Latin officior (“to perform a function”) and of Medieval Latin officiō (“to officiate, say mass (9th cent.); to serve a church (13th cent.); to serve (early 13th c., 14th in British sources); to discharge an office (14th c.)”), from Latin officium (“official duty, service”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). The noun is derived from Medieval Latin officiātus (“monk in charge of a monastic office, official (start of 12th c., 14th in British sources)”), substantivized from the participle, see -ate (noun-forming suffix).
examples: She officiated as registrar at the wedding.
She officiated the wedding as registrar.

senses: Often preceded by set: in or into flames; so as to be burned by fire.
In or into a colour like that of a flame.
In or into a state of great activity or emotion (anger, excitement, etc.).
ety: The adjective is derived from the adverb, which is attested earlier.
examples: The low sun had set aflame the numerous windows of a large building which turned slowly, demonstrating one huge chimney, then another, as the train clattered by.
He who sent (If He sent) all those hearts aflame?

senses: Food, especially for livestock.
ety: From Middle English provendre, from Old French provendre, variant of provende (“allowance, provision”), from Late Latin praebenda (“a payment, in Medieval Latin also an allowance of food and drink, pittance, also a prebend”). Doublet of prebend.
examples: The farm which supplied to him ungrudging provender had all his vast capacity for work in willing exercise …
He ripp'd the womb up of his mother, / Dame Tellus, 'cause he wanted fother, / And provender, wherewith to feed / Himself and his less cruel steed.
Irregular, sporadic feeding and strange provender were beginning to take their toll, and I felt queasy at the thought of 'various curries' the Amat's clerk had promised for the first meal of the day.

senses: A space which is alien to what is normal within the society, variably presenting a utopian vision in physical form or serving to segregate subversive elements from the wider society.
ety: From hetero- + -topia.
examples: Michel Foucault gave the museum and the mental hospital as two different examples of heterotopias.

For Foucault, heterotopias are not imagined places but real places that almost delete themselves from public consciousness. They are null sites in awareness, yet inevitable and vital to the construction of space.

senses: Somewhat fat, pudgy, overweight.
ety: From an archaic sense of port (“manner in which a person carries himself; bearing; deportment; carriage”) + -ly.
examples: In the length he attains, and in his baleen, the Fin-back resembles the right whale, but is of a less portly girth, and a lighter colour, approaching to olive.
His portly middle section, rising beyond like a small hill, heaved rhythmically.

In Heavyweights, Tony Perkis (Ben Stiller) is a fitness guru who installs himself as the über-buff leader of Camp Hope, with the goal of helping portly youngsters shed their saggy stomachs and thunder thighs.

senses: A person who consumes no animal flesh with the exception of fish or seafood.
ety: Blend of Italian pesce (“fish”) + vegetarian.
examples: Eat for Immunity follows a plant-based approach to improving immunity that is relevant to every style of eating—carnivore, pescetarian, vegetarian and vegan.

senses: The optical analogue of radar, using intense pulses of laser light to measure the composition and structure of the atmosphere.
A device that provides such imaging.
ety: By anacronymic evolution from LIDAR.
examples: Tesla bet on the idea that in the design of self-driving cars, lidar doesn't add enough capability, beyond what the cameras already provide, to be worth the additional cost.
There's a lidar mounted on the roof of that Waymo.

senses: Synonym of decade, a ten-year period.
A tenth anniversary, particularly
Synonym of decennalia, the festival and religious ritual held in the 10th year of a Roman emperor's reign.
ety: From Latin decennialis, from decennium (“10-year period”) + -ālis, from decennis (“10-year”) + -ium (“-ium”, suffix forming abstract nouns), from decem (“ten”) + annus (“year”) + -is (suffix forming compound adjectives).
examples: Roman coins mentioning the vota publica for Macrinus are RIC IV.1 5–13; on vota publica for the decennials and vicennials of emperors in the 2nd and 3rd c. ad, see Chastagnol 1984.
